planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; set the crown at soil level and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

directions: Janet Fisk is an older, long-cultivated Pulmonaria saccharata selection grown for its distinctive apple-green leaves overlaid with dense, frosty-silver marbling that runs nearly edge to edge rather than forming discrete spots. In early spring it produces small clusters of funnel-shaped flowers that open pink from pink-tinged buds and mature to blue, giving a two-toned effect typical of the genus. Like other lungworts it is a tough, deer- and rabbit-resistant groundcover for shaded beds, but it is prone to powdery mildew if the soil dries out in summer, so consistent moisture and air circulation matter more for this cultivar than for sun-tolerant modern hybrids. Shear off tattered foliage after flowering to encourage a cleaner flush of fresh leaves for the rest of the season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Lachskonigin Astilbe (Salmon Queen, Light Pink Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lachskonigin (German for 'Salmon Queen') tolerates more sun than many astilbes if soil stays consistently moist.

directions: Lachskonigin is one of the classic Georg Arends astilbe hybrids, bred in Germany and still grown for its soft, light salmon-pink plumes that rise well above a mound of finely divided, dark green compound foliage in midsummer. The color is gentler and more pastel than many modern red or magenta astilbe cultivars, making it a useful bridge tone between hot colors and whites in a mixed shade border. It shares the genus's demand for constant moisture and rich organic soil, and will scorch or go dormant early if allowed to dry out during bloom. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain strong flowering, and mulch annually to conserve soil moisture through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade or filtered sun; Amerika is drought-intolerant and will decline quickly if the soil is allowed to dry out.

directions: Amerika is a vigorous, long-established Arendsii-group astilbe producing dense, conical plumes of fuchsia-pink flowers held above toothed, mid-green divided foliage in midsummer. It is among the more cold-tolerant astilbe cultivars, shrugging off hard winter freezes without dieback issues, but it shares the genus's intolerance of dry soil and hot, exposed sites. Site it in a streamside bed, pond margin, or any consistently damp shaded spot where it can be combined with ferns, hostas, or ligularia for a layered woodland-edge planting. Deer tend to leave it alone, and clumps benefit from division every three to four years in early spring to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Feuer Astilbe (Fire, Bumalda Red Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade or filtered sun; Feuer (also sold as 'Fire' or under the older name 'Bumalda') blooms later in the season than many red astilbe cultivars.

directions: Feuer is an old Arendsii-group astilbe cultivar, also sold in English-language markets as 'Fire', valued for its warm, glowing red plumes that open from midsummer into early fall, later than most of the arendsii hybrids. The glossy, finely cut foliage emerges with a bronzy-red tint in spring before settling into mid-green, giving the clump two seasons of color interest beyond the bloom period. It performs best with reliably moist, rich soil and benefits from afternoon shade in hotter climates, where full sun exposure combined with dry soil will scorch the foliage. Its late bloom window makes it useful for extending the astilbe display after earlier cultivars like Fanal or Deutschland have finished; divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous.
sources: European nursery trade references (Lorberg, Bruns Pflanzen)

common_name: Rosa Perle Astilbe (Rose Pearl, Bright Pink Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Rosa Perle (sold in some markets as 'Rose Pearl') tolerates full sun only where soil never dries out.

directions: Rosa Perle is a classic Arendsii-group astilbe producing bright, vivid pink plume-like flower spikes over mounds of ferny, dark green divided foliage from early to midsummer. It is among the more compact and cold-hardy arendsii cultivars, shrugging off severe winter freezes without crown damage, which has kept it in circulation in European and North American nursery catalogs for decades despite newer introductions. Give it moist, fertile soil and partial shade; it is more sun-tolerant than many astilbes but only where soil moisture is dependable, and it will wilt and brown quickly in dry conditions. Use it toward the front of a shaded or pond-edge border where its shorter stature shows off the dense flower color, and divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Birthday Cake Heucherella (Chocolate-Lavender Deeply Cut Foamy Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Birthday Cake is a patented Terra Nova Nurseries introduction (US Plant Patent PP16,158) bred by Dan Heims.

directions: Birthday Cake is a compact, vigorous heucherella whose deeply lobed, almost finely dissected leaves recall its tiarella parentage in shape while carrying the rich chocolate-brown-to-lavender coloring and bold maroon veining typical of heuchera. In late spring it sends up airy spikes of small creamy-white flowers well above the tidy mounded foliage, and the foliage itself continues to shift in hue through the season as temperatures change. It tolerates more sun than many foamy bells, making it a flexible choice for the edge of a bed that gets a few hours of direct light, though color and vigor are best in consistently moist, well-drained soil. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall, and pair it with ferns, hostas, or dark-leaved heuchera for foliage contrast in a shaded border.
